name: Cherry Servers
summary: A Lithuanian host that rents dedicated bare-metal servers through an API, billed by the hour, as spot capacity or by the month, from seven locations in Europe, the US and Asia.
intro: Cherry Servers is mainly a bare-metal provider. Instant Servers are stocked dedicated machines, up to 128 cores and 768 GB of memory, that deploy in about 12 minutes; Custom Servers are built to order in one to three days, with up to 1,152 GB of memory, ten NVMe disks and optional GPUs. Next to them sit virtual servers (shared-core VPS and dedicated-core VDS, including Arm VDS), Elastic Block Storage and backup storage. Everything is driven through a REST API, the `cherryctl` CLI, Python and Go SDKs, a Terraform provider and an Ansible collection.

Servers can be billed monthly or annually in advance, or on demand by the hour. Spot servers are spare on-demand machines sold at up to 70% off; Cherry Servers can reclaim them with two minutes’ notice, which you only see by polling the server’s `termination-date` API endpoint, and the SLA doesn’t apply. Traffic is metered on outgoing data only: a fixed-term dedicated server includes 100 TB a month, allowances are pooled across a project, and extra traffic costs €0.50 per TB in Europe and the US. Singapore and Tokyo have their own, smaller allowances (20 TB for a dedicated server) and €1.69 per TB.

The company’s headquarters are in Šiauliai, Lithuania, which is also one of its server locations; the others are Amsterdam, Frankfurt, Stockholm, Chicago, Singapore and Tokyo. It accepts card payments and cryptocurrencies, and counts blockchain node operators, streaming and gaming companies among its customers.
strengths: Single-tenant hardware created and destroyed through an API and billed by the hour, which suits short jobs and CI on bare metal
Generous pooled traffic: 100 TB a month per fixed-term dedicated server in Europe and the US, at €0.50 per extra TB
Spot servers at up to 70% off for stateless, fault-tolerant work
Automation tools for the whole lifecycle: REST API, `cherryctl`, SDKs, Terraform and Ansible, with user data at deploy time
limits: A host, not a full cloud: the product list stops at servers, block storage and backups, so databases and orchestration are yours to run
Asia-Pacific traffic is much more expensive and allowances there are a fifth of Europe’s; Singapore traffic is not pooled with other regions
Spot servers can be terminated with two minutes’ notice, and the notice only shows up if you poll the API for each server
If a project goes over its traffic cap, bandwidth can be throttled to 100 Mbps until usage drops or more traffic is bought

story: Cherry Servers began in 2001 as a few college students in Lithuania who wanted to build their own IT business, trying everything from website hosting to desktop software. In 2008 they dropped the side ventures and went all in on hosting and infrastructure. In 2010 the company, then a dedicated-server host, introduced a brand for foreign markets, BalticServers, and an EU-funded project record later described it as the biggest exporter of data center services in Lithuania.

The company traded as Baltic Servers and later renamed itself Cherry Servers. It grew without outside funding, reinvesting in its product and team, and shifted toward API-driven bare metal for developers, Web3 and data-heavy teams. Locations outside Lithuania followed: Frankfurt became its sixth in February 2025, Arm VDS plans launched in Lithuania that August, and Tokyo went live in May 2026.

choices.why: In 2008 the founders stopped their side ventures because spreading effort across unrelated products slowed them down; concentrating on hosting let them improve faster and give more consistent service.
On-demand servers are paid by the hour from a prepaid team balance and spare stock is sold as spot capacity, so the same dedicated hardware can be rented for an hour or for a year.
The company says it reinvested in its product, team and customers rather than raising money, and grew steadily as a result.
